terms.gloss: a line drawn with a pen or pencil; in geometry, a line
evidence: Plin. NH 35.84: līneam dūcendō, of Apelles practising his art every day (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 1.10.41: illa circumcurrēns līnea, a line running round, a circle
Gell. 1.20.8: līnea est … longitūdō quaedam sine lātitūdine et altitūdine, Varro’s definition
Traupman 306: līneās dūcere, to draw lines
terms.comment: From līnum, flax: first a thread or a builder’s line, then a stroke of the pen or pencil. To draw one is līneam dūcere. Cicero’s trānsīre līneās, to cross the lines, is the image for going beyond the mark; for colouring in, intrā līneās and extrā līneās say it plainly, as in the examples, and Quintilian’s extrā praescrīptum ēgredī is the classical way of saying that a child’s hand strays outside the guide.

phrases.english: Colour inside the lines, if you can.
Mind you don’t go outside the lines.

phrases.latin: continēbitur enim utrimque marginibus neque extrā praescrīptum ēgredī poterit
phrases.english: for he will be held in by the edges on either side and will not be able to stray outside the guide
to do wrong is like stepping over the lines

sources: Lewis & Short: linea
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 306.
